co_flagstaff.blurb: Flagstaff sits on the slope directly above the city of Boulder and is one of the Front Range's main bouldering zones. Almost everything here is a boulder problem, from V0 into the V12 and V13 range, though most fall between V0 and V8 and the top end is thin. The rock is coarse sandstone that chews skin and can turn greasy when the day warms up, and problems often feel tougher than their numbers say. They are densely packed, many close to the road, so linking up a circuit makes a natural day. Cool, dry spring and fall conditions are favored, and sunny winter days can work too. Cloud Shadow, Red Wall and Hobo Cave are among the larger clusters, while the outlying zones are quieter than the central ones.

va_breaks_interstate_park.blurb: Breaks Interstate Park in southwest Virginia is built around a deep gorge that the Russell Fork River cut through Pine Mountain, a landscape often nicknamed the Grand Canyon of the South. The cliffs are layered, hard sandstone. Sport routes make up most of the climbing, with a substantial number of trad lines and a small handful of boulder problems. Grades run from about 5.8 to 5.13, with the bulk of the routes in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, so it suits stronger climbers best while still offering some moderates. Approaches are short and the views over the gorge are a big part of the appeal. Prospectors, Pinnacle Rock Area and Towers/Lodges are the biggest sections.

ca_indian_cove_campground.blurb: Indian Cove is the north side of Joshua Tree National Park, entered from Highway 62 and not linked by road to the rest of the park. It sits roughly 1,000 feet lower than the main park and is fairly sheltered, which makes it a good choice on cold winter days; winter, spring and fall are the comfortable seasons. Climbing is on granite that runs a little grainier than elsewhere in the park, mostly trad with a fair amount of sport, top-rope and bouldering. Grades are mainly 5.6 to 5.11, peaking around 5.10, with easier climbs too. Many walls face south and take lots of sun, and approaches are short. Campfire Crag, Feudal Wall and Short Wall are among the larger areas. Some formations end with a steep downclimb.

ut_moe_s_valley.blurb: Moe's Valley lies just west of St. George in southern Utah, a short drive from town, and is a bouldering-only destination. It is known as a winter refuge, where climbers go to escape snowy conditions at home. The stone is grainy brown and orange sandstone that wears skin down fast, and it is fragile when damp, so it needs time to dry after weather. Problems run from V0 to V14, with the most weight between V2 and V6 and a long tail of harder lines. The boulders are scattered across many zones, including Sentinel Area, Mario Land, South End and Monkey Boy Area, so a day can be spent in one cluster or moving between several.

ca_valley_south_side.blurb: Valley South Side covers the cliffs on the southern side of Yosemite Valley, a canyon cut about 3,000 feet deep into solid granite. Trad climbing dominates, with sport routes clustered at a few crags, a number of aid lines and a scattering of boulders. Roped grades mostly run from 5.7 to 5.12, centered on 5.10 and 5.11, and many of the classics are multi-pitch, some very long. Cathedral Area is the largest zone, followed by Glacier Point Apron, a big granite slab at the east end of the valley noted for its slab climbing and moderate lines. Half Dome and Leaning Tower are also part of this side, which gives it routes ranging from short crag climbs to full-day walls.

nc_linville_gorge.blurb: Linville Gorge is a rugged wilderness gorge in the North Carolina mountains, and one of the Southeast's best-known climbing destinations. The rock is quartzite, usually low-angle with few parallel cracks, so routes tend to wander and route finding matters. Nearly everything is trad, with a modest amount of sport, a little top-roping and some remote bouldering. Grades are mainly 5.9 to 5.11, with plenty of easier multi-pitch as well, which makes the gorge a reasonable place to learn longer leads. Table Rock and the Amphitheater are the usual picks for moderates, while Hawksbill and Shortoff Mountain draw climbers after harder test pieces. Distances between the sub-areas are long, so plan each day around one.
